column1: Here's the catch, and it may surprise you.
Rare earths are not actually rare.
The rare part is getting them out clean.
There are seventeen of them.
And when you dig them up, you get them mixed together.
Think of them as seventeen brothers and sisters who look almost exactly alike.
Nearly the same size, same habits, almost the same chemistry.
To your eye, and to most chemicals, they look the same.
So how do you pull one of them out of the crowd?
There's no single magic step.
You dissolve the mix in acid, and the liquid flows through a long row of tanks.
Each tank pulls them apart... only a tiny bit.
So you repeat it.
Again and again.
A big plant can run hundreds of these tanks in a row, just to get one element clean.
It's like washing rice.
One wash takes out a little dirt.
You want it perfectly clean?
You keep washing... hundreds of times.
And that's only the first half.
The second half is faster.
Let me run you through it.
Next, the clean rare earth becomes a metal.
You melt that metal with iron and boron — a mix like that is called an alloy — and cool it into thin pieces.
Then hydrogen gas cracks those pieces, and you grind them into a powder much smaller than flour.
You line that powder up inside a strong magnetic field, press it into a block, and bake it at about a thousand degrees.
Only at the very end do you switch on its magnetism.
That's when you finally have a magnet.
